concepts.definition: The smallest voltage step a 10-bit ADC can tell apart: 5 V / 1023, about 4.89 mV.
concepts.example: 2.550 V is rounded to step 522; converting it back gives 2551.3 mV, and the 1.3 mV in between is the rounding difference.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking you can measure a 1 mV change with a 10-bit ADC; the step is 4.89 mV.

concepts.definition: Small, random wobbles that get mixed into the measured voltage without anyone wanting them.
concepts.example: With the potentiometer still, in a real circuit the analogRead value wobbles 510, 513, 509.
concepts.pitfall: Assuming that because the value did not move in the lab, it will not move in a real circuit either.

concepts.definition: Shrinking noise by using the average of many readings; with N readings it drops about square-root(N) times.
concepts.example: The average of 16 readings shrinks the noise about 4 times, the average of 64 readings 8 times.
concepts.pitfall: Making the number of readings needlessly large and slowing the program down; 64 readings are 64 times the work of 1 reading.

concepts.definition: Using two separate thresholds for switching on and off, and keeping the previous decision in the region between them.
concepts.example: The LED lights when the value goes above 524 and goes off when it drops below 500; in between it stays as it is.
concepts.pitfall: Choosing a gap between the two thresholds narrower than the size of the noise; the flicker comes back.

quiz.prompt: Which of these do you really see in the lab?
options: The ADC value jittering by a few steps while the potentiometer is still
The voltage being rounded to the nearest ADC step
The supply voltage drifting from 5.00 V to 4.70 V
A button bouncing several times on one press
quiz.explanation: The lab models the ADC step: every voltage is rounded to the nearest step. Noise, reference drift and button bounce are not modelled; the lab's voltages are perfectly steady.

quiz.prompt: A 10-bit ADC divides the 0-5 V range into 1023 equal steps. About how many millivolts is one step? (Two decimal places are enough.)
quiz.explanation: 5000 mV / 1023 ≈ 4.89 mV. That is why a 10-bit ADC cannot tell 1 mV changes apart; the result is always rounded to the nearest step.

510 is below the threshold: 0. 530 > 524: it lights, 1. 515 and 505 are between the two thresholds, so the decision is kept: 1, 1. 495 < 500: it goes off, 0. 520 is inside the band again and already off: 0. The output is 011100. If you used a single threshold (512), it would also light at 515 and 520.

options: The deger variable should not have been read with analogRead
The constants should not have been const
ACMA and KAPAMA are the wrong way round: KAPAMA is bigger than ACMA, so there is no band
int should have been used instead of bool
quiz.explanation: The threshold to switch on is 510 and to switch off 514: when the value is 511 it lights, but in the same pass it goes off straight away because 511 < 514. For hysteresis, the switch-on threshold must be higher than the switch-off threshold (for example 524 and 500), and the gap between them must be bigger than the noise. The other options have nothing to do with the behaviour.

quiz.prompt: With the average of N readings, noise drops about square-root(N) times. About how many times does the average of 64 readings shrink the noise?
quiz.explanation: Square-root(64) = 8. But the cost is 64 times the work: it drops 4 times with 16 readings and 8 times with 64; the gain has diminishing returns, so making the number of readings needlessly large slows the program down.
